title: 10  Storage & Indexing
section: 10.3 Why We Need a Buffer Manager
text:
10.3 Why We Need a Buffer Manager
Whenever a database uses data, that data must exist in memory (RAM) — because the CPU can only work with data that is loaded there. Accessing data in RAM is fast (nanoseconds), but RAM is expensive and limited in size. A typical database can be hundreds of gigabytes or even terabytes, and it is simply impossible to fit all of it in memory at once.
Disks (HDDs or SSDs) solve the capacity problem — they are cheap and can store enormous amounts of data permanently. But there is a catch: accessing data on disk is thousands of times slower than accessing data in RAM.
This creates a fundamental tension:



Storage
Speed
Size
Cost




RAM
Very fast (ns)
Small
Expensive


Disk
Very slow (ms)
Huge
Cheap



The database needs a module that bridges this gap — something that:

Loads data from disk into RAM on demand (when a query needs it)
Keeps frequently used data in RAM so it does not have to be re-read from disk
Writes modified data back to disk to make it permanent
Decides which data to evict from RAM when memory is full and new data needs to come in

This is exactly the job of the Buffer Manager.
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
section: 10.4 What Does the Buffer Manager Do?
text:
10.4 What Does the Buffer Manager Do?
The DBMS buffer manager sits between RAM and disk. It maintains a pool of pages in RAM — called the database buffer — and is responsible for the following:

Allocates buffer space in main memory so that data blocks can be temporarily stored there while in use.
Returns the address of a requested data block if that block is already present in the database buffer (no disk access needed).
Fetches missing blocks from disk into the buffer when a requested data block is not currently in memory.
Evicts older blocks from the buffer when there is no free space available, making room for newly requested blocks.
Writes dirty blocks to disk before evicting them — if an evicted block was recently modified, its changes must be saved to disk first; otherwise it is simply discarded.
Re-fetches evicted blocks from disk storage back into the buffer if a user later requests data that was previously removed.


10.4.1 How It All Works Together
The diagram below traces what happens when you run a SQL query — from the moment the query arrives to when results are returned (and how modified data is synced back to disk).

















TipKey Takeaway




The first time you query data → it comes from disk (slow)
The second time you query the same data → it comes from the buffer in RAM (fast — no disk access!)
If you modify data → the change happens in the buffer first, then gets written back to disk to make it permanent









ImportantThe Page is the Unit of I/O



All disk reads and writes transfer exactly one page (typically 4–16 KB, configurable). Reading a single 10-byte row forces a full page to come into RAM. Query cost is measured in number of page I/Os, not rows accessed.
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.5 Records and Page Layout
Every table in a relational database is stored on disk. But disk and memory work differently — the CPU can only process data that is in memory (RAM), and disk stores data in fixed-size chunks. To bridge this, three concepts stack on top of each other:












A record is one row (the database’s smallest unit of meaning)
A page is a fixed-size block (the disk’s smallest unit of transfer, typically 4–16 KB)
A file is a sequence of pages that stores all records of one table

When the DBMS decides how to store a table, it must answer four questions — in this exact order:

What type of file? — heap or sorted?
How are pages organized in the file? — linked list or page directory?
How are records organized on each page? — packed, bitmap, or slotted?
How is each record formatted? — fixed-length or variable-length?



10.5.1 1 — Types of Files
The file type determines how pages (and the records inside them) are ordered. The DBMS picks the type that gives the lowest I/O cost for the table’s typical workload.

1 I/O = reading or writing exactly 1 page between disk and memory.


Heap File — “Throw it anywhere”
Records and pages are stored in no particular order. New records go into any page that has free space.














Operation
Cost (N = number of pages)




Full scan
N


Search by key
N (must scan everything)


Insert
≈ 2 (find a free page + write it)


Delete
Search cost + 1 write




✅ Very cheap inserts
❌ Search always costs a full scan



Sorted File — “Keep it in order”
Pages are ordered and records within each page are sorted by a key field. This makes binary search possible.
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  Sorted File  (sorted by ID)                          │
│  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐           │
│  │  Page 1  │  │  Page 2  │  │  Page 3  │  ...      │
│  │  ID: 1   │  │  ID: 51  │  │  ID: 101 │           │
│  │  ID: 2   │  │  ID: 52  │  │  ID: 102 │           │
│  │  ...     │  │  ...     │  │  ...     │           │
│  │  ID: 50  │  │  ID: 100 │  │  ID: 150 │           │
│  └──────────┘  └──────────┘  └──────────┘           │
│  Records always in sorted order → binary search works │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘







Operation
Cost (N = number of pages)




Full scan
N


Search by key
\log_2 N (binary search)


Insert
\log_2 N + N (find spot + shift records to maintain order)


Delete
\log_2 N + N




✅ Fast searches
❌ Expensive inserts — shifting records to keep order can touch every page







TipWhich file type should you use?



Choose based on the most common operation:

Mostly inserts + full scans (e.g., logs, events) → Heap File
Mostly searches by key (e.g., user lookup by ID) → Sorted File

In practice, most real tables use heap files and add indexes (like B+ trees) on top to speed up searches without the insert cost of sorted files.






10.5.2 2 — How Pages Are Organized in a File
Regardless of file type, the DBMS must track which pages have free space for inserting new records. There are two standard implementations:

Linked List Implementation
A header page at the start points to two separate linked lists of data pages:

Full pages list — pages that have no room left
Free pages list — pages that still have space

Each data page stores pointers to the next and previous pages in its list, plus a free-space tracker.
┌─────────────────┐
│   Header Page   │
└────┬────────────┘
     │
     ├──→  Full Pages:  [Page 3] ←→ [Page 1] ←→ [Page 6] ←→ ...
     │
     └──→  Free Pages:  [Page 5] ←→ [Page 2] ←→ [Page 4] ←→ ...
                         ↑
                    (has free space)
To insert a new record: scan the free-pages list until a page with enough room is found.

✅ Simple to implement
❌ In the worst case, you must scan all free pages — expensive when the file is large



Page Directory Implementation
Only the header pages are linked together. Each header page holds a list of entries, where each entry says: “Data page X has Y bytes of free space”.
┌──────────────────┐      ┌──────────────────┐
│   Header Page 1  │ ───→ │   Header Page 2  │ ───→ ...
│                  │      │                  │
│ [Page 1 | 120B]  │      │ [Page 4 | 400B]  │
│ [Page 2 |   0B]  │      │ [Page 5 |  88B]  │
│ [Page 3 |   0B]  │      │ [Page 6 | 212B]  │
└──────────────────┘      └──────────────────┘
        ↓                         ↓
  (data pages              (data pages
   stored here)             stored here)
To insert a new record: read header pages only — each entry already tells you how much space is available on each data page. No need to touch data pages at all until you find the right one.

✅ Much faster than linked list for inserts
✅ Scales well — even with thousands of pages, you only read a few header pages







ImportantCounting I/Os with Header Pages



When a question gives you the specific implementation (linked list or page directory), include header page reads in your I/O count. If no implementation is specified, ignore header page cost.






10.5.3 3 — How Records Are Organized on a Page
Now we look inside one page. How are the individual records laid out? The answer depends on whether records are fixed-length or variable-length.

Pages with Fixed-Length Records
Every record is the same size, so the DBMS knows exactly where each one is. Two layouts exist:
Packed layout — records are stored back-to-back with no gaps.
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Page Header (# records = 3)                   │
├──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬─────────────┤
│ Record 1 │ Record 2 │ Record 3 │  Free Space  │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴─────────────┘
  ← records grow this way →          ↑ next insert goes here

Insert: next position = (# records) × (record size)
Delete: must shift all later records left by one to fill the gap (keeps it packed)

Unpacked layout (Bitmap) — the page header stores a bitmap. Each bit = one slot. 1 = occupied, 0 = free.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Page Header  [bitmap: 1 1 0 1 0 0 ...]             │
├──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬──────────┬────────┤
│ Record 1 │ Record 2 │  empty   │ Record 4 │  ...   │
└──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴──────────┴────────┘
                            ↑
                    slot 3 is free (bit = 0)

Insert: find first 0 bit → write record there → set bit to 1
Delete: set that slot’s bit to 0 — no shifting needed



Pages with Variable-Length Records (Slotted Page)
When records can have different sizes (e.g., VARCHAR fields), a slotted page layout is used. The key idea is:

Records are stored from the top of the page downward
A slot directory lives at the bottom of the page and grows upward
Free space stays in the middle between records and slot directory

┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐  ← top of page
│           Page Header                        │
│  (page_id, free space pointer, ...)          │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Record 1  (e.g., 42 bytes)                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Record 2  (e.g., 28 bytes)                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  Record 3  (e.g., 55 bytes)                 │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│           F R E E   S P A C E              │
│                                             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ ... │ (ptr₃, len₃) │ (ptr₂, len₂) │ (ptr₁, len₁) │ free ptr │ slot count │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘  ← bottom of page
                ↑  Slot Directory (grows upward)
The slot directory contains:



Field
What it stores




Slot count
Total number of slots (filled + empty)


Free space pointer
Byte offset of the next free position


Entry per slot
(record pointer, record length)



Insert: write the record at the free space pointer → add a new (pointer, length) entry in the slot directory.
Delete: set the slot entry to null (pointer = null, length = null) → the space is reclaimed later during compaction (periodically, live records are repacked to merge gaps).






NoteWhy use a slot directory?



Every record is identified by a Record ID = (page number, slot number). Indexes store these Record IDs to point to records. If a record moves within the page (e.g., during compaction), only its slot entry changes — the Record ID stays the same. This keeps all indexes valid without any updates.






10.5.4 4 — Record Formats
This is the innermost level: how are the bytes of a single record laid out?

Fixed-Length Records (FLR)
Every field has a known, fixed size. All records of the same schema occupy exactly the same number of bytes.
Schema: Employee(id INTEGER, age INTEGER, salary FLOAT, active BOOLEAN)

┌──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────────┬──────────┐
│  id          │  age         │  salary      │  active  │
│  4 bytes     │  4 bytes     │  4 bytes     │  1 byte  │
└──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────────┴──────────┘
 offset 0       offset 4       offset 8       offset 12

Total record size = 4 + 4 + 4 + 1 = 13 bytes (every record, always)
To find field i: \text{offset} = \sum_{j=0}^{i-1} \text{size}(j)
Standard field sizes:



Type
Size




INTEGER
4 bytes


FLOAT
4 bytes


BOOLEAN
1 byte


CHAR(N)
N bytes


DATE
8 bytes


VARCHAR(N)
≤ N bytes (variable!)




✅ Simple and fast — no overhead needed
❌ CHAR(50) storing "Ali" wastes 47 bytes



Variable-Length Records (VLR)
A VLR contains at least one variable-length field (VARCHAR, TEXT). Since we don’t know the exact size at schema time, the record uses a record header to store pointers to the end of each variable-length field. Fixed-length fields always come first.
Schema: Person(name VARCHAR(20), age INTEGER, city VARCHAR(15))

┌─────────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────────────┐
│   Record Header     │  Fixed Fields │  Variable Fields      │
│  (end-of-var ptrs)  │  age: 4 bytes │  name  │  city        │
│  [ptr_name|ptr_city]│               │  "Ali" │  "Cairo"     │
└─────────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────────────┘
                                         ↑ actual bytes stored
                                         only 3 + 5 = 8 bytes,
                                         not 20 + 15 = 35 bytes
Layout rule: fixed-length fields first, then variable-length fields in order.

✅ Space-efficient — stores only what is needed
❌ Requires reading the record header to find variable fields







Note



Regardless of format, every record has a unique Record ID = (page #, slot #) that the DBMS uses to locate it directly from disk.











FLR
VLR




Field sizes
All fixed
Mix of fixed + variable


Record size
Same for all records
Varies per record


Example fields
INT, FLOAT, CHAR(N)
VARCHAR, TEXT


Find field i
Offset = sum of prior sizes
Read record header first


Space usage
May waste space
Uses only what’s needed






10.5.5 Solved Example — Page Capacity and Scan Cost






Note📝 Solved Example



Problem: An Employee table has 80,000 records. Each record is fixed-length with the following fields:



Field
Size




Ssn
9 bytes


Fname
15 bytes


Lname
15 bytes


Salary
8 bytes


Dno
4 bytes



Page size = 4 KB (4,096 bytes). Page header occupies 96 bytes.
(a) How many records fit on one page? (b) How many pages does the table occupy? (c) What is the I/O cost of a full table scan?
Solution:
(a) Record size = 9 + 15 + 15 + 8 + 4 = 51 bytes
Usable space per page = 4096 − 96 = 4000 bytes
\text{Records per page} = \left\lfloor \frac{4000}{51} \right\rfloor = 78 \text{ records/page}
(b) Pages needed:
\text{Pages} = \left\lceil \frac{80{,}000}{78} \right\rceil = \left\lceil 1025.6 \right\rceil = 1026 \text{ pages}
(c) A full table scan reads every page:
\text{I/O cost} = 1026 \text{ page reads}
If a disk read takes ~5 ms, the scan takes ≈ 5.1 seconds. A B+ tree index on Ssn would reduce the same lookup to 3–4 page reads ≈ 0.02 ms.

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.6 What is Database Indexing?
Imagine a huge database as a giant list of records. Searching through this list without an index is like looking for a needle in a haystack — you’d have to check each record one by one. But with an index, it’s like having a roadmap that shows you exactly where to look!
An index in a database is a special data structure that stores pointers to the actual data in a way that makes retrieving information much faster. It’s like a catalog that helps you find what you’re looking for without scanning everything.

10.6.1 Real-Life Example: Finding a Customer’s Order
Let’s say you run an e-commerce website and you need to find a customer’s order. Your database might look like this:

10.6.2 How Search Works Without an Index






Caution❌ Full Table Scan (No Index)



To find Omar’s orders, the database must check every single row from top to bottom:

Row 1 — Ahmed? ✗   skip
Row 2 — Fatima? ✗   skip
Row 3 — Omar? ✓   found → save Row 3
Row 4 — Ahmed? ✗   skip
Row 5 — Youssef? ✗   skip
Row 6 — Layla? ✗   skip
Row 7 — Fatima? ✗   skip
Row 8 — Kareem? ✗   skip
Row 9 — Omar? ✓   found → save Row 9
Row 10 — Youssef? ✗   skip

10 rows checked to find 2 results. With 10 million rows, that means 10 million comparisons — the cost grows linearly with table size: O(n).




10.6.3 How Search Works With an Index






Tip✅ Index Lookup (With Index on Customer Name)



The index keeps Customer Name values sorted. To find Omar:

The database opens the index (a sorted structure — B+ tree).
It performs a binary search / tree traversal directly to "Omar".
It reads the stored pointer: Omar → Order IDs {2, 9}.
It fetches only those 2 rows from the data file.

2 rows fetched, ~3–4 index steps regardless of table size. Cost grows logarithmically: O(\log n).




10.6.4 Sorted Reference Table (Index Structure)
The index on Customer Name looks like this internally:



Customer Name
Order IDs




Ahmed

Kareem

10.6.5 Solved Example — Index Speedup Calculation






Note📝 Solved Example



Problem: A university has a Students table with 500,000 rows stored in a heap file. A registrar needs to find all course registrations for student S00142. The database measures:

Full table scan time: 10 seconds
B+ tree index height on student_id: h = 4
Each page read takes 0.02 ms

(a) How many page reads does the full scan require? (b) How many page reads does the indexed lookup require (assume 3 matching rows on 2 pages)? (c) What is the speedup factor?
Solution:
Assume page size 4 KB, record 100 bytes → 20 records/page.
(a) Full scan: \text{Pages} = \left\lceil \frac{500{,}000}{20} \right\rceil = 25{,}000 \text{ page reads} \text{Time} = 25{,}000 \times 0.02\,\text{ms} = 500\,\text{ms} \approx 0.5\,\text{s}
(b) Index lookup: h + data pages = 4 + 2 = 6 page reads \text{Time} = 6 \times 0.02\,\text{ms} = 0.12\,\text{ms}
(c) Speedup: \text{Speedup} = \frac{25{,}000}{6} \approx 4{,}167\times \text{ faster}
This is why indexes are critical for large OLTP tables.

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.7 File Organization in Indexing
File organization refers to how data and indexes are physically stored in memory or on disk. The choice of file organization directly determines which index types are applicable, how efficiently the DBMS can locate records, and what the cost of each query operation will be.
The following are the common types of file organizations used in indexing:

10.7.1 Heap File






NoteHeap Organization



Records are stored in insertion order — no sorting, no grouping. New rows are simply appended to the end of the file.

Access: Full table scan required to find any record → O(n)
Best for: Bulk loading data, write-heavy tables, full-table analytics
Index compatibility: Any index type can be built on top of a heap file; the index itself provides the ordering
Limitation: Without an index, every query reads every page

Heap File (unsorted):
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ Fatima | Laptop   | 1200 │  ← inserted first
│ Omar   | Headsets | 150  │
│ Ahmed  | Phone    | 500  │
│ Layla  | Watch    | 200  │  ← inserted last
└──────────────────────────┘




10.7.2 Sequential (Sorted) File






NoteSequential Organization



Records are stored sorted by a key (the ordering field). Finding a record by that key can use binary search.

Access: Binary search on ordering key → O(\log n) pages
Best for: Range queries on the sort key (WHERE salary BETWEEN 3000 AND 7000)
Index compatibility: A sparse index works perfectly — one index entry per page block
Limitation: Insertions are expensive (must maintain sort order); only one sort order possible

Sequential File (sorted by Customer Name):
┌──────────────────────────┐
│ Ahmed  | Phone    | 500  │  ← A
│ Fatima | Laptop   | 1200 │  ← F
│ Kareem | Monitor  | 400  │  ← K
│ Omar   | Headsets | 150  │  ← O  ← binary search lands here
│ Youssef| Camera   | 700  │  ← Y
└──────────────────────────┘




10.7.3 Hash File






NoteHash Organization



Records are placed into buckets determined by a hash function h(\text{key}) \mod B, where B is the number of buckets.

Access: Equality lookup → O(1) theoretical (one bucket access)
Best for: Exact-match equality queries (WHERE id = 42)
Index compatibility: Pairs naturally with a hash index
Limitation: Range queries are impossible — hashing destroys sort order; overflow buckets degrade performance

Hash File (hash on Order ID, B = 3):
Bucket 0: │ Order 3 │ Order 6 │ Order 9  │
Bucket 1: │ Order 1 │ Order 4 │ Order 7  │ Order 10 │
Bucket 2: │ Order 2 │ Order 5 │ Order 8  │




10.7.4 Clustered File






NoteClustered Organization



Records are physically stored in the same order as the primary index (usually a B+ tree). The data file is the index leaf level.

Access: Range queries read consecutive pages → minimizes I/O
Best for: Range queries + sorted output on the clustering key
Index compatibility: The table can have only one clustered index (one physical sort order)
MySQL InnoDB: Every table is always a clustered B+ tree ordered by the primary key

Clustered File (clustered on Customer Name):
B+ Tree leaf pages:
Page 1: │ Ahmed, Phone, $500 │ Ahmed, Tablet, $300 │
Page 2: │ Fatima, Laptop, $1200 │ Fatima, Keyboard, $100 │
Page 3: │ Kareem, Monitor, $400 │ Layla, Watch, $200 │
Page 4: │ Omar, Headsets, $150 │ Omar, Charger, $50 │




10.7.5 Summary: File Organizations at a Glance

10.7.6 Solved Example — Choosing a File Organization






Note📝 Solved Example



Problem: A hospital Patients table stores 200,000 records. The following query patterns are observed:



Query

Very high (lookup by PK)


WHERE age BETWEEN 30 AND 50

Recommend a file organization and justify your choice for each query.
Solution:

Recommended Organization
Justification




Equality on patient_id
Clustered (B+ tree on patient_id)
O(\log n) — primary key lookup; InnoDB auto-clusters on PK

Range scan is O(\log n + k) with sorted file or B+ tree

Tip



In MySQL InnoDB, the table is always physically a clustered B+ tree on the primary key. All other access patterns are served by secondary unclustered indexes.

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.8 Index Concepts
An index is an auxiliary data structure that maps search key → record location (RID). It is separate from the data file and maintained automatically on INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE.

10.8.1 Index Entry Structure: Key → Value
Every entry in an index is a key–value pair:







Component
What it holds




Key (search key)
A copy of the indexed column(s) value — e.g., "Charlie", 42, "2024-01-15"


Value (data reference)
A pointer to the actual row(s) in the main table — the Record ID (RID) = (page_id, slot_id)









NoteWhat the index actually stores




Copies of selected column values (the search key) — not the full row
Pointers to the actual data rows in the main table (RIDs), so the DBMS can fetch the full record when needed
The structure stays sorted (B+ tree) or hashed, allowing fast lookups without scanning the entire table

This is why adding an index trades a little extra storage and write overhead for dramatically faster reads.















10.8.2 Taxonomy

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.9 Types of Indexing Methods
Indexes are classified along three independent dimensions: density, clustering, and key type. Understanding these helps you choose the right index for each query pattern.

10.9.1 Dense vs. Sparse Index

Dense IndexSparse Index


A dense index has one index entry for every record in the data file.

Works on any file organization (heap or sorted)
Faster lookup — every record has a direct pointer
Higher storage cost — index grows with the data

Data File          Dense Index
───────────        ────────────────────
Ahmed  | p1,s1  ←  Ahmed  → (p1,s1)
Fatima | p1,s2  ←  Fatima → (p1,s2)
Kareem | p2,s1  ←  Kareem → (p2,s1)
Omar   | p2,s2  ←  Omar   → (p2,s2)


A sparse index has one index entry per page (data block), not per record.

Requires the data file to be sorted on the index key
Much smaller index — fits in fewer pages
Lookup: find the correct page via index, then scan within the page

Data File (sorted)   Sparse Index
──────────────────   ─────────────────
Page 1: Ahmed        Ahmed  → page 1
        Fatima       Kareem → page 2
Page 2: Kareem       Omar   → page 3
        Layla
Page 3: Omar
        Youssef









Note



B+ trees in practice use a hybrid approach: sparse at internal levels (routing keys only), dense at the leaf level (one pointer per record).




10.9.2 Clustered vs. Unclustered Index






ImportantClustered Index



The physical order of data rows matches the index order. Reading a range of index entries also reads consecutive pages.

A table can have only one clustered index
In MySQL InnoDB, the primary key is always the clustered index
Secondary indexes store the primary key as their RID — one extra lookup per row (“index dive”)


10.10 Unclustered Index
The index order does not match the data order. Each index pointer may point to a different page.

Many unclustered indexes allowed per table
Range queries may cause one page I/O per row — expensive at scale













Clustered
Unclustered




Range query (k rows)
~k / records_per_page pages
Up to k separate pages


Equality query
~height pages
~height pages


Build cost
High (file must be sorted)
Lower


Count per table
Only one
Many allowed





10.10.1 Primary vs. Secondary Index








Type
Defined on
Key property




Primary index
The ordering key of a sequential/clustered file
One entry per distinct key value; non-duplicate


Secondary index
Any non-ordering attribute
Can have duplicate keys; always unclustered unless it matches the physical order









Tip



A secondary index is the workhorse of OLTP systems — it allows fast lookup on any column (email, phone, status) without reorganizing the data file.




10.10.2 Solved Example — Clustered vs. Unclustered I/O Cost






Note📝 Solved Example



Problem: An Employee table has 40,000 records stored across 2,000 pages (20 records/page). Department 4 (Dno = 4) has 4,000 employees.

In the clustered case: all Dno=4 employees occupy consecutive pages.
In the unclustered case: the 4,000 employees are randomly scattered (worst case: one per page).
B+ tree height h = 3 for both indexes.

Compute the I/O cost for: SELECT * FROM Employee WHERE Dno = 4
Solution:
Clustered B+ tree index on Dno: \text{Pages for Dno=4} = \left\lceil \frac{4{,}000}{20} \right\rceil = 200 \text{ pages} \text{Total I/O} = h + \text{data pages} = 3 + 200 = \mathbf{203} \text{ page reads}
Unclustered B+ tree index on Dno: \text{Worst case: each matching record on a different page} \text{Total I/O} = h + 4{,}000 = 3 + 4{,}000 = \mathbf{4{,}003} \text{ page reads}








Index Type
I/O Cost
Notes




Clustered
203 reads
Sequential pages — disk-friendly


Unclustered
up to 4,003 reads
Random I/O — 20× more expensive


Full scan (no index)
2,000 reads
Cheaper than unclustered for large selectivity!









Important



When selectivity is high (many matching rows), the optimizer may choose a full scan over an unclustered index because random I/O becomes more expensive than sequential I/O.

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.11 B-Tree and B+ Tree Index
Both B-Tree and B+ Tree are self-balancing tree structures used to keep data sorted and allow searches, insertions, and deletions in O(\log n) time. They are the foundation of indexing in virtually every major RDBMS.

10.11.1 B-Tree vs. B+ Tree: Key Differences








Feature
B-Tree
B+ Tree




Data pointers
In all nodes (internal + leaf)
Leaf nodes only


Internal nodes
Store keys and data records
Store keys only (routing)


Leaf nodes
Not linked
Linked as a doubly-linked list


Range queries
Slower — may visit internal nodes
Fast — scan leaf chain sequentially


Space efficiency
Lower (data in every node)
Higher (internal nodes hold more keys → larger fan-out)


Used in practice
Rare (mostly theoretical)
MySQL, PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server









NoteWhy B+ Tree Won



Because internal nodes in a B+ Tree store only keys (no data), each internal node can hold far more keys — increasing the fan-out and reducing the tree height. A B+ Tree with order d = 100 over 100 million records has only 4 levels. Range scans are also trivial: follow the leaf chain without backtracking through the tree.




10.11.2 B+ Tree Structure

Balanced: all leaf nodes at the same depth h; guarantees O(\log n) operations
Order d: every internal node except the root holds between d and 2d search keys
All data pointers in leaves: internal nodes hold only keys for routing
Leaf chain: leaf nodes are linked in a doubly-linked list for sequential range scans














10.11.3 Cost Analysis








Operation
I/O Cost
Formula




Equality search
h page reads
h = \lceil \log_d n \rceil


Range scan (k results)
h + \lceil k / f \rceil
f = records per leaf page


Insert
$h + $ splits
Amortised O(1) splits


Delete
$h + $ merges
Rare in practice



Example: order d = 100, n = 10^8 records → h = \lceil \log_{100} 10^8 \rceil = 4 levels. Four page reads to find any record in a 100-million-row table.


10.11.4 Solved Example — B+ Tree Height and Search Cost






Note📝 Solved Example



Problem: A Transactions table has 50 million records. A B+ tree index of order d = 200 is built on the TransactionDate column. Each leaf page holds 200 records.
(a) Calculate the tree height h. (b) What is the I/O cost for an equality query (find transactions on a specific date, 5 matching records)? (c) What is the I/O cost for a range query returning 10,000 transactions? (d) How does this compare to a full table scan (20 records/page)?
Solution:
(a) Tree height: h = \left\lceil \log_{2d}\, n \right\rceil = \left\lceil \log_{400}\, 50{,}000{,}000 \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{\log 50{,}000{,}000}{\log 400} \right\rceil = \left\lceil \frac{7.699}{2.602} \right\rceil = \lceil 2.96 \rceil = \mathbf{3 \text{ levels}}
(b) Equality search (5 rows on 1–2 leaf pages): \text{I/O} = h + \text{leaf pages} = 3 + 1 = \mathbf{4 \text{ page reads}}
(c) Range scan (10,000 rows, 200 rows/leaf page): \text{Leaf pages} = \left\lceil \frac{10{,}000}{200} \right\rceil = 50 \text{I/O} = h + 50 = 3 + 50 = \mathbf{53 \text{ page reads}}
(d) Full table scan: \text{Pages} = \left\lceil \frac{50{,}000{,}000}{20} \right\rceil = 2{,}500{,}000 \text{ page reads}

Relative cost

625,000×

10.14 Hash Indexes
A hash index applies a hash function h(k) to map a key to a bucket where matching records are stored.














Characteristic

Buckets chain when full




10.14.1 Extendible Hashing
Uses a global depth and a directory. When a bucket overflows: 1. Split only the full bucket (not all buckets) 2. Double the directory only when all buckets at that depth are full
Hash indexes are available as USING HASH in PostgreSQL and as MEMORY storage engine indexes in MySQL.

10.15.3 When to Use Bitmap Indexes






Tip



Bitmap indexes are ideal for:

Low-cardinality columns: Gender, Status, Region (few distinct values → compact bitmaps)

Avoid bitmap indexes on: - High-cardinality columns (every value different → one bit vector per row = huge overhead) - OLTP tables with frequent writes — bit vectors must be updated on every INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE

10.16 Index Selection Guidelines

10.16.1 When to Create an Index







Create index when…
Avoid when…




Column frequent in WHERE predicates
Table has fewer than a few thousand rows


Column used in JOIN … ON condition
Column has very low cardinality (boolean, status with 2 values) — consider bitmap


Column in ORDER BY or GROUP BY
Table is write-heavy (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) — index maintenance overhead


Foreign key column (speeds up deletes of parent)
Column almost never queried alone


Covering index candidate (all SELECT cols in index)
Index is redundant with another existing index





10.16.2 Composite (Multi-Column) Index

MySQLPostgreSQLOracle


-- Index on (Dno, Salary) — useful for filtering by dept and sorting by salary
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dno_sal ON Employee(Dno, Salary);

-- A covering index: includes all columns needed by the query (avoids table lookup)
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_cover ON Employee(Dno, Salary, Fname, Lname);

-- Verify index usage
EXPLAIN SELECT Fname, Lname, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Dno = 5 ORDER BY Salary DESC;


CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dno_sal ON Employee(Dno, Salary);

-- Partial index: only index rows matching a condition (smaller, faster for sparse predicates)
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_mgr ON Employee(Super_ssn) WHERE Super_ssn IS NOT NULL;

-- Functional index (index on expression)
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_lower_lname ON Employee(LOWER(Lname));

-- Verify
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT Fname, Lname, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Dno = 5 ORDER BY Salary DESC;


CREATE INDEX idx_emp_dno_sal ON Employee(Dno, Salary);

-- Function-based index
CREATE INDEX idx_emp_upper_lname ON Employee(UPPER(Lname));

-- Bitmap index for low-cardinality column
CREATE BITMAP INDEX idx_emp_sex ON Employee(Gender);

-- Verify (execution plan)
EXPLAIN PLAN FOR SELECT Fname, Lname, Salary FROM Employee WHERE Dno = 5 ORDER BY Salary DESC;
SELECT * FROM TABLE(DBMS_XPLAN.DISPLAY);

title: 10  Storage & Indexing
text:
10.17 Chapter Summary






ImportantKey Takeaways — Chapter 10




All disk I/O transfers pages (4–16 KB). The buffer manager caches pages; the cost metric is page reads.
File organizations: heap (insertion order), sequential (sorted), hash, clustered. MySQL InnoDB stores data in the clustered B+ tree (primary key order).
Dense vs sparse: dense index has one entry per record; sparse index has one entry per page (requires sorted file).
B+ tree: balanced, fan-out 2d, height h \approx \log_d n. All leaves linked for range scans. Supports equality, range, ORDER BY, and GROUP BY efficiently. With d = 100 and 10^8 records: only 4 page reads to find any record.
Hash index: O(1) equality; completely useless for range queries.
Bitmap index: per-distinct-value bit vectors; bitwise AND/OR answering multi-predicate analytical queries at CPU speed. Best for low-cardinality columns in OLAP.
Composite indexes: leftmost prefix rule determines which predicates the index covers. A covering index includes all columns a query needs — eliminates all table lookups.
Use EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE to verify that the optimizer selects the intended index.

10.18 Review Questions

10.18.1 Conceptual

Why is the page the unit of I/O instead of the row? How does this influence the cost of a full table scan versus an index scan?

What is the tree height h?

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.1 The Journey of a SELECT
In Chapter 10 you learned where data lives (pages, B+ trees, bitmap bitmaps). In Chapter 6 you learned what operations transform data (relational algebra). This chapter connects them: how does a DBMS take your SELECT and produce a result efficiently?
The answer is a four-stage pipeline that every major RDBMS follows.
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.2 Query Processing Pipeline












11.2.1 Stage 1 — Parser
Verifies syntax; produces a parse tree.
SELECT E.Fname FROM Employee E WHERE E.Salary > 50000
→ parse tree: Project(Filter(Scan(Employee), Salary>50000), [Fname])


11.2.2 Stage 2 — Rewriter

Replaces view references with the view’s stored SELECT
Applies semantic simplifications (e.g., NOT (x > 5) → x <= 5)
Produces the initial relational algebra expression



11.2.3 Stage 3 — Optimizer
The core of this chapter. Given the algebra expression, the optimizer:

Applies equivalence rules to generate alternative expressions (logical optimization)
Selects physical algorithms for each operator (physical optimization)
Estimates the cost of each candidate plan using statistics from the system catalog
Returns the plan with the lowest estimated total cost



11.2.4 Stage 4 — Execution Engine
Executes the physical plan: - Fetches pages via the buffer manager - Applies operators using pipelining or materialization - Returns rows to the client
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.3 Translation to Relational Algebra
SELECT E.Fname, D.Dname
FROM   Employee E
       JOIN Department D ON E.Dno = D.Dnumber
WHERE  E.Salary > 50000;
Initial (naive) algebra expression:

\pi_{\text{Fname, Dname}}\bigl(\sigma_{\text{Salary}>50000}(\text{Employee} \times \text{Department})\bigr)

After pushing the selection down and converting to a join:

\pi_{\text{Fname, Dname}}\bigl(\sigma_{\text{Salary}>50000}(\text{Employee}) \bowtie_{\text{Dno=Dnumber}} \text{Department}\bigr)

This is better — the filter reduces Employee rows before the join (fewer rows to join).
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.4 Logical Optimization: Equivalence Rules
The optimizer systematically applies these rules to push work closer to the leaves:








Rule
Description
Benefit




R1 — Selection commutativity
\sigma_c(R) = \sigma_c(R)
Trivially true


R2 — Selection cascade
\sigma_{c_1 \wedge c_2}(R) = \sigma_{c_1}(\sigma_{c_2}(R))
Split complex condition


R3 — Selection push-down (join)
\sigma_c(R \bowtie S) = \sigma_c(R) \bowtie S when c only involves R
Reduce R early


R4 — Projection push-down
Keep only needed columns early
Reduce row width


R5 — Join commutativity
R \bowtie S = S \bowtie R
Choose smaller outer


R6 — Join associativity
(R \bowtie S) \bowtie T = R \bowtie (S \bowtie T)
Reorder joins freely



Before vs After optimization (expression trees):
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.5 Cost Model
The optimizer estimates every operator’s I/O cost using catalog statistics.

11.5.1 Key Statistics








Statistic
Symbol
Meaning




Pages
B(R)
Number of disk pages in relation R


Tuples
T(R)
Number of rows


Distinct values
V(A,R)
Number of distinct values of attribute A


Selectivity
\text{sel}(A=v)
Fraction of rows matching A=v — assumed 1/V(A,R)





11.5.2 Operator Cost Estimates







Operator
I/O cost estimate




Sequential scan
B(R)


Equality with clustered B+ tree
\lceil B(R) / V(A,R) \rceil


Equality with unclustered index
up to T(R) / V(A,R)


Sort (M buffer pages)
2 B(R) \cdot (1 + \lceil \log_{M-1}(\lceil B(R)/M \rceil) \rceil)


Hash join
3\,(B(R) + B(S))


Block nested-loop join (M buffers)
\lceil B(R)/(M-2) \rceil \cdot B(S) + B(R)









Tip



Total cost = I/O cost + CPU cost. In most systems with spinning disks, I/O dominates. On NVMe SSDs, CPU cost becomes more relevant — some modern optimizers model both.
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.6 Selection Algorithms

11.6.1 Sequential Scan
Read every page of R: cost = B(R).
Use when: no index, or the filter is not selective enough to justify random I/O.
Turning point: an unclustered index becomes worse than a full scan when the selectivity is above ~5–10% (because random I/Os exceed the savings).


11.6.2 Binary Search (Sorted File)
\lceil \log_2 B(R) \rceil page reads. Rarely used standalone — only when file is sorted on the search key.


11.6.3 B+ Tree Index Scan
σ_{Salary = 55000}(Employee)
  → Clustered B+ tree on Salary
  → h page reads (path) + ⌈B(R)/V(Salary, Employee)⌉ pages at leaf level
Range query σ_{Salary > 50000}(Employee): - Clustered: traverse leaf chain — sequential I/O, very efficient - Unclustered: each record may require a separate random I/O — potentially worse than a full scan for high selectivity
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.7 Join Algorithms
Joins are the most expensive operation. Three fundamental algorithms:

11.7.1 Nested-Loop Join
for each tuple r in R (outer):
    for each tuple s in S (inner):
        if r.key = s.key: output (r, s)








Variant
Cost
Notes




Naïve NLJ
T(R) \cdot B(S) + B(R)
Inner scanned once per outer tuple


Block NLJ (M buffers)
\lceil B(R)/(M-2) \rceil \cdot B(S) + B(R)
Inner scanned once per outer block


Index NLJ
B(R) + T(R) \cdot C_{idx}
Uses index on inner; C_{idx} ≈ 3–5 for B+ tree





11.7.2 Sort-Merge Join
Phase 1: External sort R on join key → R'   (cost: 2 B(R) per pass)
Phase 2: External sort S on join key → S'   (cost: 2 B(S) per pass)
Phase 3: Merge R' and S' once              (cost: B(R) + B(S))
Total cost ≈ 3(B(R) + B(S)) for the common two-pass case.
Benefits: excellent when data is already sorted, or when the output needs to be sorted (avoids a second sort).


11.7.3 Hash Join
Build phase:   partition R into h buckets via h1(key)
Partition:     partition S into same h buckets via h1(key)
Probe phase:   for each bucket i:
                   load R_i into memory hash table
                   probe with every s in S_i
Cost = 3(B(R) + B(S)) (two passes over each relation: read/write partitions, then probe).
SQL: two records r, s can only match if h_1(r.k) = h_1(s.k) — only matching buckets need to be compared.


11.7.4 Algorithm Selection Guide







Algorithm
Best When




Index NLJ
One relation small; other has index on join key


Block NLJ
Small outer relation; inner has no index


Sort-Merge
Data already sorted; output needs to be sorted; both large


Hash Join
Large unsorted equijoins; no useful sort or index
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.8 Pipeline vs Materialization
When executing a multi-operator plan, the engine can transmit rows between operators in two ways:









Strategy
Description
Memory
Speed




Pipelining
Operator passes a row immediately to the parent as soon as it produces it
Low — one row at a time
Faster — no intermediate writes


Materialization
Operator writes its entire result to a temp table; parent then reads it
High — full intermediate
Slower — extra I/O, but sometimes required



Materialisation is required when: - The operator needs the full input before producing output (e.g., external sort, hash-build phase, DISTINCT, GROUP BY) - The result is used multiple times (e.g., an inner relation in a nested-loop join)
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.9 EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE
EXPLAIN shows the optimizer’s chosen plan without executing the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE executes the query and reports both estimated and actual statistics.

MySQLPostgreSQL


EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE
SELECT E.Fname, D.Dname
FROM   Employee E
       JOIN Department D ON E.Dno = D.Dnumber
WHERE  E.Salary > 50000;
Sample output:
-> Nested loop inner join
   -> Filter: (e.Salary > 50000)  (cost=2.75 rows=4)
       -> Index range scan on e using idx_emp_salary  (cost=2.75 rows=4)
   -> Single-row index lookup on d using PRIMARY (Dnumber=e.Dno)  (cost=0.25 rows=1)
-- EXPLAIN ANALYZE — adds actual rows and execution time
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT E.Fname, D.Dname
FROM   Employee E JOIN Department D ON E.Dno = D.Dnumber
WHERE  E.Salary > 50000;


EXPLAIN (FORMAT TEXT, ANALYZE, BUFFERS)
SELECT E.Fname, D.Dname
FROM   Employee E
       JOIN Department D ON E.Dno = D.Dnumber
WHERE  E.Salary > 50000;
Sample output:
Hash Join  (cost=12.50..98.75 rows=150 width=64)
            (actual time=0.542..1.203 rows=4 loops=1)
  Hash Cond: (e.dno = d.dnumber)
  Buffers: shared hit=8
  ->  Index Scan using idx_emp_salary on employee e
        (cost=0.43..85.00 rows=200 width=40)
        (actual time=0.124..0.311 rows=4 loops=1)
        Index Cond: (salary > 50000)
  ->  Hash  (cost=8.00..8.00 rows=360 width=24)
            (actual time=0.287..0.287 rows=3 loops=1)
        ->  Seq Scan on department d  (cost=0.00..8.00 rows=360 width=24)
                                      (actual time=0.019..0.047 rows=3 loops=1)
Planning Time: 0.312 ms
Execution Time: 1.421 ms




11.9.1 Reading an EXPLAIN Output

Bottom-up: leaf nodes (scans) execute first; their output feeds parent joins
cost=start..total: estimated startup and total cost in arbitrary optimizer units
rows=n: estimated output rows (compare with actual rows= to spot bad estimates)
actual time=x..y ms: wall-clock time for first/last row (loops=n means the node repeated n times)
Buffers: shared hit=n (PostgreSQL): pages served from buffer cache (no disk I/O)







ImportantWhen Estimates ≠ Actuals



If rows=200 but actual rows=4, the optimizer had stale or missing statistics. Fix: run ANALYZE Employee; (PostgreSQL) or ANALYZE TABLE Employee; (MySQL) to refresh statistics.

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
section: 11.10 Putting It All Together: A Worked Plan
text:
11.10 Putting It All Together: A Worked Plan
-- Q: Names + total hours for Research dept employees working > 20 h
SELECT   E.Fname, E.Lname, SUM(WO.Hours) AS TotalHours
FROM     Employee E
         JOIN Works_On   WO ON E.Ssn     = WO.Essn
         JOIN Project    P  ON WO.Pno    = P.Pnumber
         JOIN Department D  ON P.Dnum    = D.Dnumber
WHERE    D.Dname = 'Research'
GROUP BY E.Ssn, E.Fname, E.Lname
HAVING   SUM(WO.Hours) > 20;
Optimized plan (conceptual):











Key optimization choices: 1. Selection on Department pushed down (only 1 row matches Dname='Research') — eliminates 3 of 4 departments before any join
2. Join order: small filter result joined first; large Employee table joined last
3. GROUP BY after all joins — only grouped once, not per-join

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.11 Chapter Summary






ImportantKey Takeaways — Chapter 11




Pipeline: SQL → Parser (parse tree) → Rewriter (algebra) → Optimizer (physical plan) → Execution Engine (result).
Logical optimization applies equivalence rules to push selections/projections toward leaves, reorder joins, and reduce intermediate result sizes before choosing algorithms.
Cost model uses catalog statistics (B(R), T(R), V(A,R)) to estimate I/O. Refresh with ANALYZE when estimates diverge from actuals.
Three join algorithms:

Nested-loop: simple; best with a small outer + index on inner
Sort-merge: best when data is sorted or output needs to be sorted
Hash join: default for large unsorted equijoins; cost ≈ 3(B(R)+B(S))

Pipelining passes rows between operators on-the-fly (low memory, faster); materialization writes full intermediate results to disk (required for sort, GROUP BY, DISTINCT).
EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows the actual plan, estimated vs actual rows, and execution time. A large discrepancy between estimated and actual rows signals stale statistics.

text:
11.13 Query Processing Pipeline
SQL Query (text)
      │
  ┌───▼─────────┐
  │   Parser    │  → Syntax check, build parse tree
  └───┬─────────┘
      │ Parse tree
  ┌───▼──────────────┐

  └───┬──────────────┘

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.14 Parsing and Translation
The parser checks SQL syntax and builds a parse tree. The translator converts it to an initial relational algebra (RA) expression:
SELECT e.fname, d.dept_name
FROM employee e JOIN department d ON e.dept_no = d.dept_no
WHERE e.salary > 50000;
Translates to:

\pi_{\text{fname, dept\_name}}\bigl(\sigma_{\text{salary} > 50000}(\text{employee} \bowtie_{\text{dept\_no}} \text{department})\bigr)
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.15 Query Optimization Overview
The optimizer’s job: find the cheapest execution plan from the many equivalent RA expressions.

11.15.1 Why Optimization Is Hard

A join of n tables has O(n!) possible orderings (actually more, counting bushy trees)
For 5 tables: 5! = 120 plans; for 10 tables: 10! = 3,628,800 plans
Cost depends on: table sizes, selectivities, index availability, memory



11.15.2 Two Phases of Optimization

Logical optimization: Apply algebraic equivalences to improve the RA tree (push selections down, push projections)
Physical optimization: Choose algorithms for each logical operator (which join algorithm? which access path?)
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.16 Cost Model
The optimizer uses a cost model to estimate the cost of each plan:

\text{Total Cost} = \text{I/O cost} + \text{CPU cost} + \text{Communication cost}

In most systems: I/O cost dominates (disk access >> CPU).
Cost factors per operator:



Operator
Key cost factor




Sequential scan
B(R) pages


Index scan (clustered)
B(R) / V(A, R) pages


Index scan (unclustered)
Up to T(R) / V(A, R) page I/Os


Sort
2 B(R) \cdot (1 + \lceil \log_M B(R) \rceil)


Hash join
3 (B(R) + B(S))


Nested loop join
B(R) + T(R) \cdot B(S) (worst case)



Where: - B(R) = number of pages in relation R - T(R) = number of tuples in R - V(A, R) = number of distinct values of attribute A in R - M = number of buffer pages available

11.16.1 Statistics in the System Catalog
The optimizer reads statistics to estimate costs: - B(R): page count - T(R): tuple count - V(A, R): domain cardinality (distinct values) - Histogram: distribution of attribute values
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.17 Selection Algorithms

11.17.1 Linear Scan (Sequential Scan)
Read every page of the table: cost = B(R).
Use when: no usable index exists.


11.17.2 Binary Search
On sorted file: cost = \lceil \log_2 B(R) \rceil.


11.17.3 Index-Based Selection
Equality: σ_{A = v}(R)
├── Clustered B+ tree: cost ≈ height + B(R)/V(A,R) pages
└── Unclustered B+ tree: cost ≈ height + T(R)/V(A,R) page I/Os (potentially many)

Range: σ_{A ≥ v}(R)
├── Clustered B+ tree: height + fraction of pages  (efficient)
└── Unclustered B+ tree: may be slower than full scan if many matches
crumbs: Part VI: Storage, Indexing & Query Processing

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.18 Join Algorithms
Joins are the most expensive operations. Three fundamental algorithms:

11.18.1 1. Nested-Loop Join (NLJ)
for each tuple r in R:           ← outer relation
    for each tuple s in S:       ← inner relation
        if r[join_attr] = s[join_attr]: output (r, s)

Cost: T(R) \cdot B(S) + B(R) page I/Os (inner scanned once per outer tuple)
Choose the smaller relation as outer to minimize cost
Improved by block nested loop: read a block of outer relation at a time



11.18.2 2. Sort-Merge Join (SMJ)
Phase 1: Sort R on join attribute → R'
Phase 2: Sort S on join attribute → S'
Phase 3: Merge R' and S' (like merge sort)

Cost: 2 B(R) + 2 B(S) + B(R) + B(S) = sort costs + merge cost
Excellent when both relations are already sorted, or when the output also needs to be sorted
Only scans each relation once during merge



11.18.3 3. Hash Join
Phase 1 (Build):   Partition R into h buckets using hash function h1
Phase 2 (Partition): Partition S into same h buckets using h1
Phase 3 (Probe):   For each bucket i, build in-memory hash table on R_i,
                   then probe with every tuple in S_i

Cost: 3(B(R) + B(S)) for the standard case
Best when at least one relation fits in memory after partitioning
Most efficient for large unsorted equijoins



11.18.4 Algorithm Comparison









Algorithm
Best Case
Worst Case
Good When




Nested Loop
One relation fits in mem: B(R) + B(S)
T(R) \cdot B(S)
Small tables, inner has index


Sort-Merge
B(R) + B(S) (pre-sorted)
Sort cost + merge
Data pre-sorted, output sorted


Hash Join
B(R) + B(S) (build fits in mem)
3(B(R)+B(S))
Large unsorted equijoins

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.19 Join Ordering and Plan Enumeration

11.19.1 Left-Deep vs. Right-Deep vs. Bushy Trees
Left-deep:          Right-deep:          Bushy:
    ⋈                   ⋈                    ⋈
   / \                 / \                  / \
  ⋈   D             A    ⋈                ⋈    ⋈
 / \                     / \              / \  / \
⋈   C                   B    ⋈           A  B  C  D
/ \                          / \
A   B                       C   D
Most optimizers enumerate only left-deep trees (n-1 levels deep) — this reduces the search space from (2n-2)! / (n-1)! to n!.


11.19.2 Dynamic Programming Optimization
For each subset of relations S: 1. Find the optimal plan for accessing each single relation 2. For each pair, find optimal join order 3. Build up bottom-up
This finds the global optimum in O(3^n) time instead of O(n!).

title: 11  Query Processing & Optimization
text:
11.20 Query Plan Reading (EXPLAIN)
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT e.fname, d.dept_name
FROM employee e
JOIN department d ON e.dept_no = d.dept_no
WHERE e.salary > 50000;
Sample output:
Hash Join  (cost=12.50..98.75 rows=150 width=64)
  Hash Cond: (e.dept_no = d.dept_no)
  ->  Index Scan using idx_emp_salary on employee e
        (cost=0.43..85.00 rows=200 width=40)
        Index Cond: (salary > 50000)
  ->  Hash  (cost=8.00..8.00 rows=360 width=24)
        ->  Seq Scan on department d  (cost=0.00..8.00 rows=360 width=24)
Reading the plan: - The tree is read bottom-up — innermost operations happen first - cost=start..total: estimated startup and total cost (in page I/Os) - rows=n: estimated number of output rows - -> denotes a child operator feeding into its parent






Tip



Always run EXPLAIN ANALYZE (not just EXPLAIN) to see actual rows and execution times as well as estimates.

text:
11.21 Summary






ImportantChapter 11 — Key Takeaways




Query pipeline: Parse → Rewrite → Optimize → Execute.
The optimizer applies algebraic equivalences (push σ down, reorder joins) and selects physical algorithms.
Cost model relies on catalog statistics (B(R), T(R), V(A,R)) to estimate I/O.

Left-deep trees reduce the plan search space; dynamic programming finds the optimal join order.

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.1 Why Transactions?
Chapters 7–8 showed you how to read and write data with SQL. But two problems arise in any real system:
Transactions solve both problems: they provide an atomic, isolated unit of work with guaranteed durability after commit and recovery after failure.

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
Multi-step operations must either complete fully or not at all — a bank transfer that deducts money but never credits the recipient would be catastrophic.
Concurrent access by many users can corrupt data if writes interfere with reads — without coordination, two users booking the last airline seat could both succeed.

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.2 What Is a Transaction?
A transaction is a sequence of one or more SQL operations that the DBMS treats as a single, indivisible unit of work.
Example — Bank Transfer of $500 from Account A to Account B:
BEGIN;                                                          -- start transaction
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Id = 'A';
    UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Id = 'B';
COMMIT;                                                         -- make permanent
If the system crashes after the first UPDATE but before the second, the DBMS rolls back the first update automatically — money never disappears.

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.3 ACID Properties







Property
One-line definition




Atomicity
All-or-nothing: every operation in a transaction commits together or none do


Consistency
A transaction moves the database from one consistent (valid) state to another


Isolation
Concurrent transactions are invisible to each other; execute as if serial


Durability
Once committed, changes survive crashes, power loss, and restarts




12.3.1 Worked Examples — What Goes Wrong Without Each Property

Without AtomicityWithout ConsistencyWithout IsolationWithout Durability


-- T1: Transfer $500 A → B
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 500 WHERE Id = 'A';   -- success
-- ** crash here ** — second update never runs
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 500 WHERE Id = 'B';

-- Result: $500 vanishes; A debited, B never credited
-- Fix: atomicity guarantees the first update is undone too


-- Business rule: total balance across all accounts must remain constant
-- T1 withdraws $500 from A and deposits $600 to B (bug in code)
-- After commit: total balance increased by $100 — DB is inconsistent
-- Fix: consistency ensures constraints and business rules hold post-commit


-- T1: Read A = 500, prepare to add 100
-- T2: Read A = 500, prepare to add 200, commits: A = 700
-- T1: commits: A = 600  ← T2's update is overwritten — lost update!
-- Fix: isolation serialises T1 and T2 so one runs fully before the other reads


-- T1 commits: "Salary updated"
-- ** power failure 2 ms after response sent to client **
-- System restarts: salary reverted to old value
-- Fix: durability requires the committed write to survive any failure

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.4 Transaction States


















State
Description




Active
Transaction is executing; reads/writes in progress


Partially Committed
COMMIT issued; log record written but not yet flushed to stable storage


Committed
Log flushed; changes durable; normal end


Failed
Cannot proceed — error or explicit ROLLBACK BEGIN


Aborted
All changes undone; database restored to pre-transaction state

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.5 Concurrency Anomalies
When multiple transactions run without coordination, four classes of anomaly can occur.

12.5.1 Lost Update
Two transactions both read a value, modify it independently, and write back — the second write overwrites the first.



Time
T1
T2
X value




t1
Read X

100


t2

Read X
100


t3
X ← X − 50; Write X=50

50


t4

X ← X + 30; Write X=130
130



Correct result should be 80. T1’s update is lost.


12.5.2 Dirty Read (Reading Uncommitted Data)
T1: Write(X = 200)    -- not yet committed
T2:   Read(X) = 200   -- reads T1's uncommitted value
T1: ROLLBACK          -- X reverts to 100
T2: uses X = 200      -- now based on data that never officially existed


12.5.3 Non-Repeatable Read
T1: Read(X) = 100
              T2: Write(X = 200), COMMIT
T1: Read(X) = 200   -- same query, different result within same transaction


12.5.4 Phantom Read
T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE Salary > 50000  →  10
              T2: INSERT employee with Salary = 80000, COMMIT
T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE Salary > 50000  →  11  -- new row "appeared"

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.6 Isolation Levels
SQL:1992 defines four standard isolation levels, each preventing progressively more anomalies.









Isolation Level
Dirty Read
Non-Repeatable Read
Phantom Read




READ UNCOMMITTED
✗ Possible
✗ Possible
✗ Possible


READ COMMITTED
✓ Prevented
✗ Possible
✗ Possible


REPEATABLE READ
✓ Prevented
✓ Prevented
✗ Possible (MySQL: ✓)


SERIALIZABLE
✓ Prevented
✓ Prevented
✓ Prevented




MySQLPostgreSQLOracle


-- View current level
SELECT @@transaction_isolation;

-- Change for the session
SET SESSION TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;

-- Change for next transaction only
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
BEGIN;
    -- ...
COMMIT;
MySQL InnoDB default: REPEATABLE READ (with MVCC preventing phantoms too)


SHOW transaction_isolation;

-- Per-transaction
BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
    -- ...
COMMIT;

-- Or: SET at start of transaction
BEGIN;
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE;
    -- ...
COMMIT;
PostgreSQL default: READ COMMITTED


-- Per-session
ALTER SESSION SET ISOLATION_LEVEL = SERIALIZABLE;

-- Per-transaction
SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED;
    -- ...
COMMIT;
Oracle supports only READ COMMITTED and SERIALIZABLE (no READ UNCOMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ).

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.7 Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
WAL is the mechanism that implements both Atomicity (rollback) and Durability (recovery after crash).
Core WAL rule:
> Before a modified data page is written to disk, its log record must reach stable storage first.

12.7.1 Log Record Format
Each write operation appends a record to the sequential log:
LSN  |  TxnId  |  PageId  |  Before-Image  |  After-Image  |  PrevLSN







Field
Meaning




LSN
Log Sequence Number — monotonically increasing ID


TxnId
Which transaction performed this write


PageId
Which data page was modified


Before-Image
Value before the change (needed for UNDO)


After-Image
Value after the change (needed for REDO)


PrevLSN
Pointer back to previous log record of this transaction (forms a chain)





12.7.2 Commit Flow with WAL

















ImportantSteal / No-Force Policy



Most modern DBMS use Steal + No-Force:







Policy
Meaning




Steal
Dirty (uncommitted) pages can be written to disk before commit — needed to free buffer space


No-Force
Dirty pages are not forced to disk at commit time — better write performance



This maximises performance but requires recovery to handle both: - UNDO: steal means uncommitted data may be on disk → must undo after crash - REDO: no-force means committed data may still be in buffer → must redo after crash

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.8 Recovery: Undo and Redo
After a crash, the recovery manager reads the log and restores a consistent state.

12.8.1 ARIES Recovery Algorithm (3 Phases)



















Phase
Direction
Purpose




Analysis
Forward from checkpoint
Determine what needs REDO / UNDO


Redo
Forward from earliest dirty page
Re-apply all operations (even of crashed txns)


Undo
Backward for each loser transaction
Roll back uncommitted changes





12.8.2 Checkpointing
Checkpoints reduce recovery time by: 1. Flushing all dirty pages to disk (fuzzy checkpoint: writes a checkpoint record without full flush) 2. Writing a checkpoint log record noting which transactions were active
After a crash, recovery only needs to examine log records from the last checkpoint — not the entire log.

title: 12  Transaction Processing
12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.10 Chapter Summary






ImportantKey Takeaways — Chapter 12




A transaction is an atomic unit of work: all operations succeed together or all are undone. SQL syntax: BEGIN → (operations) → COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
ACID = Atomicity (all-or-nothing), Consistency (rules preserved), Isolation (concurrent txns appear serial), Durability (committed = permanent).
Four concurrency anomalies — Lost Update, Dirty Read, Non-Repeatable Read, Phantom Read — caused by unsynchronised concurrent transactions.
Isolation levels (weakest to strongest): READ UNCOMMITTED → READ COMMITTED → REPEATABLE READ → SERIALIZABLE. Default: MySQL=REPEATABLE READ, PostgreSQL/Oracle=READ COMMITTED.
WAL (Write-Ahead Logging): log record flushed to stable storage before data page modified on disk. Implements both undo (rollback/crash) and redo (ensure committed writes survive).
ARIES recovery: three phases — Analysis (identify active txns) → Redo (replay log forward) → Undo (rollback losers backward).
Savepoints allow partial rollback without aborting the full transaction.

Space overhead

title: 12  Transaction Processing
12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.13 ACID Properties







Property
Definition




Atomicity
All operations in a transaction succeed, or none do. No partial execution.


Consistency
A transaction takes the database from one consistent state to another. Business rules preserved.


Isolation
Concurrent transactions execute as if they were serial. Intermediate states not visible to others.


Durability
Once a transaction is committed, its effects survive system failures (written to stable storage).

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.14 Transaction States
                ┌─────────────────────────────┐
                │                             │
   BEGIN        │                             │  COMMIT
─────────►  ACTIVE ─────────────────► PARTIALLY_COMMITTED ──────► COMMITTED
               │                             │
     (error/   │                  (error/    │
      ROLLBACK) │                   crash)   │
               ▼                             ▼
            FAILED ──────────────────────► ABORTED







State
Description




Active
Transaction is executing


Partially committed
Final statement executed; awaiting commit


Committed
Transaction successfully completed; changes made permanent


Failed
Normal execution can no longer proceed


Aborted
Transaction rolled back; database restored to pre-transaction state


Terminated
Either committed or aborted; leaves the system

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.15 Concurrency Issues
When multiple transactions run concurrently without control, several anomalies can arise:

12.15.1 1. Lost Update
T1: Read(X=100)                     T2: Read(X=100)
T1: X = X - 50 = 50
T1: Write(X=50)
                                    T2: X = X + 30 = 130
                                    T2: Write(X=130)   ← T1's update is lost!
Result: X=130 (should be X=80)


12.15.2 2. Dirty Read (Temporary Update)
T1: Write(X=200)                    T2: Read(X=200)   ← reads uncommitted data
T1: ROLLBACK → X restored to 100
                                    T2: uses X=200     ← wrong! dirty read


12.15.3 3. Unrepeatable Read
T1: Read(X=100)
                                    T2: Write(X=200), COMMIT

T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE salary>50000  → 10
                                    T2: INSERT new employee with salary=80000, COMMIT
T1: SELECT COUNT(*) WHERE salary>50000  → 11  ← phantom row appeared!

12.17 Concurrency Control: Two-Phase Locking (2PL)
Two-Phase Locking is the most widely used protocol for guaranteeing serializability.

12.17.1 Lock Types








Lock
Symbol

12.17.3 2PL Protocol
A transaction follows two strict phases:
Phase 1 — Growing Phase:    locks can be ACQUIRED; none released
Phase 2 — Shrinking Phase:  locks can be RELEASED; none acquired

                   Lock Point
                      │
Locks acquired ───────╯╲──────── Locks released
(growing)                        (shrinking)
Theorem: Any schedule produced by 2PL transactions is conflict-serializable (guaranteed correct).


12.17.4 Strict 2PL
A common variant: all locks are held until COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

Prevents cascading rollbacks (no dirty reads)
Used by most real DBMS implementations

-- Locks in practice (explicit locking in PostgreSQL)

-- ... process rows ...

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.18 Deadlocks
A deadlock occurs when two or more transactions wait for each other’s locks indefinitely:
T1 holds X(A), waits for X(B)
T2 holds X(B), waits for X(A)
         ↕ circular wait → deadlock

12.18.1 Deadlock Detection
Build a wait-for graph: - Node per transaction - Edge T_i \to T_j if T_i is waiting for a lock held by T_j - A cycle in the graph means deadlock
T1 → T2 (T1 waits for T2)
T2 → T3 (T2 waits for T3)
T3 → T1 (T3 waits for T1) ← cycle! deadlock
Resolution: Abort one transaction in the cycle (the “victim”) — choose by: - Youngest transaction (minimum work lost) - Transaction with fewest locks - Transaction that has not been a victim recently


12.18.2 Deadlock Prevention

Wait-Die: older transactions wait; younger ones die (rollback and restart)
Wound-Wait: older transactions wound (abort) younger ones; younger ones wait

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.19 Recovery: Logging and ARIES

12.19.1 Why Recovery Is Needed

System crash: server power loss, OS failure
Transaction abort: application error, deadlock victim
Media failure: disk crash



12.19.2 Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
WAL rule: Before any data page is written to disk, the corresponding log record must be written to stable storage first.
Every operation writes a log record:
(LSN, TransactionID, PageID, Before-Image, After-Image, PrevLSN)


12.19.3 Commit Protocol
Transaction decides to COMMIT
    ↓
Write COMMIT log record to disk (WAL)
    ↓
Transaction is durable (even if crash occurs now)
    ↓
Write modified data pages to disk (may be deferred — "steal/no-force")

title: 12  Transaction Processing
text:
12.20 Summary






ImportantChapter 12 — Key Takeaways




A transaction is an atomic unit of work; it’s the fundamental unit of DB reliability.
ACID properties: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability — enforced by the DBMS.
Concurrency anomalies: Lost Update, Dirty Read, Unrepeatable Read, Phantom Read.
Isolation levels (weakest to strongest): READ UNCOMMITTED → READ COMMITTED → REPEATABLE READ → SERIALIZABLE.
Two-Phase Locking (2PL): ensures conflict-serializability; Strict 2PL holds all locks until commit.
Deadlocks arise from circular lock waits; detected via wait-for graphs; resolved by aborting a victim.
WAL (Write-Ahead Logging): log record written before data page — ensures durability.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.1 From Problem to Protocol
Chapter 12 identified four concurrency anomalies (lost update, dirty read, non-repeatable read, phantom read) and four isolation levels that prevent them. This chapter explains how DBMS implementations actually achieve isolation: by controlling the schedule in which operations execute.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.2 Schedules
A schedule (or history) S is a total ordering of all operations from a set of concurrent transactions that preserves the intra-transaction order within each transaction.

13.2.1 Notation



Symbol
Meaning




r_i(X)
Transaction T_i reads item X


w_i(X)
Transaction T_i writes item X


c_i
Transaction T_i commits


a_i
Transaction T_i aborts





13.2.2 Serial vs Concurrent

S_{\text{serial}}: \quad r_1(A)\; w_1(A)\; c_1 \;\mid\; r_2(A)\; w_2(A)\; c_2


S_{\text{concurrent}}: \quad r_1(A)\; r_2(A)\; w_1(A)\; w_2(A)\; c_1\; c_2

A serial schedule is always correct by definition (no interference) but gives zero concurrency. The goal of concurrency control is to allow non-serial schedules that are still equivalent to some serial schedule.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.3 Conflict Serializability

13.3.1 Conflicting Operations
Two operations conflict iff: 1. They belong to different transactions 2. They access the same data item X 3. At least one is a write



Pair
Type
Conflict?




r_i(X), r_j(X)
Read-Read
No — both only read


r_i(X), w_j(X)
Read-Write
Yes


w_i(X), r_j(X)
Write-Read
Yes


w_i(X), w_j(X)
Write-Write
Yes





13.3.2 Conflict-Equivalent Schedules
Schedules S and S' are conflict-equivalent iff one can be transformed into the other by swapping adjacent non-conflicting operations.
A schedule is conflict-serializable iff it is conflict-equivalent to some serial schedule.


13.3.3 Precedence (Serialization) Graph
Build a directed graph from schedule S: - One node per transaction - Add edge T_i \to T_j if T_i has a conflicting operation that precedes an operation of T_j
Theorem: S is conflict-serializable \iff its precedence graph is acyclic (contains no cycle).


13.3.4 Worked Example

S: r_1(A)\;\; w_2(A)\;\; w_1(A)\;\; r_2(B)\;\; w_2(B)\;\; c_1\;\; c_2

Identify conflicts: - r_1(A) before w_2(A): Read-Write → edge T_1 \to T_2 - w_2(A) before w_1(A): Write-Write → edge T_2 \to T_1











The graph has a cycle (T_1 \to T_2 \to T_1) → S is NOT conflict-serializable.






Tip



If the graph were acyclic, the topological sort of the graph gives the equivalent serial order.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.4 View Serializability
View serializability is a weaker (more permissive) criterion than conflict serializability. Two schedules are view-equivalent iff:

If T_i reads the initial value of X in S, it also does so in S'
If T_i reads a value of X written by T_j in S, same in S'
If T_i performs the final write of X in S, same in S'

Every conflict-serializable schedule is view-serializable.
Not every view-serializable schedule is conflict-serializable.
View serializability is NP-complete to test → not used in practice.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.5 Recoverability

13.5.1 Recoverable Schedules
A schedule is recoverable iff: if T_j reads data written by T_i, then T_i must commit before T_j commits.
Non-recoverable example:



Time
T1
T2




t1
w_1(X)=200



t2

r_2(X)=200 (dirty read)


t3

c_2 ←** T2 commits based on T1’s data**


t4
a_1 ←** T1 aborts**




T2 committed based on data that T1 never committed. Irrecoverable — we cannot undo T2.


13.5.2 Cascading Rollback
If T1 aborts and T2 has read T1’s data, T2 must also abort — this cascades to T3 if T3 read T2’s data:
T1 aborts → T2 must abort → T3 must abort → ...


13.5.3 Cascadeless Schedules
In a cascadeless schedule, no transaction reads uncommitted data:

\text{If } T_j \text{ reads } X \text{ written by } T_i, \text{ then } T_i \text{ commits before that read}

Cascadeless \supset strict (no reading OR writing uncommitted data).

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.7 Deadlocks
A deadlock is a circular wait where each transaction holds a lock that another transaction is waiting for.

13.7.1 Wait-For Graph
Build a directed graph where edge T_i \to T_j means “T_i is waiting for T_j to release a lock.”
Deadlock iff the wait-for graph contains a cycle.











This three-way cycle is a deadlock. The DBMS detects it by running cycle detection on the wait-for graph (periodically or immediately on lock request).


13.7.2 Deadlock Resolution
Once detected, abort one transaction (the victim). Selection criteria:



Criterion
Strategy




Minimum work done
Abort the youngest transaction


Minimum cost to restart
Abort the one with fewest locks


Starvation prevention
Never choose the same victim twice









Important



After aborting a victim, the DBMS restarts the transaction automatically (usually). The application must be prepared to retry its transaction on deadlock.




13.7.3 Deadlock Prevention Strategies
Instead of detection + abort, prevent cycles from forming:








Strategy
Rule
Characteristic




Wait-Die
Old waits for young; young dies (aborts, restarts)
Non-preemptive victim choice


Wound-Wait
Old wounds (preempts) young; young waits
Fewer aborts for old transactions


No-Wait
Never wait; abort immediately if lock unavailable
Low deadlock overhead; high abort rate

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.8 Timestamp-Based Concurrency Control
Every transaction receives a timestamp TS(T) at start. Two additional timestamps are maintained per data item X:

R\_TS(X): timestamp of the last transaction that successfully read X
W\_TS(X): timestamp of the last transaction that successfully wrote X


13.8.1 Rules








Operation
Condition
Action




r_i(X)
TS(T_i) < W\_TS(X)
Abort T_i — it would read a future-written value


r_i(X)
TS(T_i) \geq W\_TS(X)
OK; set R\_TS(X) = \max(R\_TS(X), TS(T_i))


w_i(X)
TS(T_i) < R\_TS(X)
Abort T_i — its write would overwrite data already read by a newer transaction


w_i(X)
TS(T_i) < W\_TS(X)
Thomas Write Rule: skip this write (it’s already obsolete, no abort needed)


w_i(X)
otherwise
OK; set W\_TS(X) = TS(T_i)



Advantage: No deadlocks (no waiting for locks).
Disadvantage: Long-running transactions may repeatedly abort and restart (starvation).

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.9 Multiversion Concurrency Control (MVCC)
MVCC is used by the majority of modern DBMS (PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, Oracle, CockroachDB).

13.9.1 Core Idea
Each write creates a new version of the item; old versions are retained for a period. Each read sees the snapshot of the database as of its transaction’s start time — a read never blocks a write and a write never blocks a read.
Item X versions:
  v1: value=100,  created by T1 (TS=1),  expired by T5 (TS=5)
  v2: value=150,  created by T5 (TS=5),  active (never expired)

Transaction T_3 (TS=3): reads v1 (the version valid at TS=3)
Transaction T_7 (TS=7): reads v2 (the version valid at TS=7)



13.9.2 MVCC and Isolation Levels








Level
MVCC snapshot point
Blocks on writes?




READ COMMITTED
Beginning of each SQL statement
No


REPEATABLE READ
Beginning of the transaction
No


SERIALIZABLE (PG SSI)
Beginning + conflict detection
Only on detected write-write conflict



PostgreSQL’s Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) extends MVCC with anti-dependency detection, achieving true serializable isolation with minimal blocking overhead.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.10 Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)
OCC assumes conflicts are rare — so validate only at commit time rather than locking proactively.

13.10.1 Three Phases







Phase
Activity




Read
Execute transaction in a local workspace; read from DB, write to workspace; no locks


Validate
Check if any conflict exists between this transaction’s reads/writes and concurrently committed transactions


Write
If valid: apply workspace changes to DB; if invalid: abort and restart



OCC is ideal for read-heavy, low-conflict workloads. It can cause high abort rates under write-heavy contention.

title: 13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
13  Concurrency Control & Scheduling
text:
13.12 Chapter Summary






ImportantKey Takeaways — Chapter 13




A schedule is a total ordering of operations from concurrent transactions. Serial schedules are always correct; concurrent schedules need validation.
Conflict serializability (the practical standard): a schedule is correct iff its precedence graph is acyclic. An acyclic graph’s topological sort gives the equivalent serial order.
Recoverable schedules: T_j commits only after all T_i whose data it read. Cascadeless schedules: no dirty reads at all — prevents cascading rollback.
Two-Phase Locking (2PL): acquire all locks in the growing phase; release in the shrinking phase. Strict 2PL (hold X locks until commit) is what real DBMS implement. Produces conflict-serializable, cascadeless schedules.
Deadlocks: circular lock-wait chains; detected via wait-for graph cycles. Resolved by aborting a victim; prevented by Wait-Die or Wound-Wait timestamp ordering.
MVCC: readers never block writers, writers never block readers. Each transaction reads a snapshot valid at its start time. Used by PostgreSQL (with SSI for SERIALIZABLE), MySQL InnoDB, Oracle.
OCC: validate at commit, not during execution — best for low-conflict, read-heavy workloads.
